_meta.description: Rule-based knowledge base for the SmartCoop Health Checker. Every symptomWeights key MUST exist in symptoms.json (the 14 checkboxes in the existing UI) — nothing outside that checklist is ever scored. priorityOverride forces a minimum priority regardless of score, used for notifiable diseases (Newcastle Disease, Avian Influenza) where the Philippines requires DA/BAI reporting even on a moderate symptom match.
_meta.note: Weights and guidance text are a starting rule base grounded in standard PH backyard poultry disease references. Verify against a DA-BAI or veterinary source before citing in the paper.

diseases.name: Infectious Bronchitis
recommendedActions: Isolate birds showing respiratory signs from the rest of the flock.
Ensure good ventilation in the coop without creating cold drafts.
Provide clean drinking water and easy access to feed.
Consult a veterinarian if breathing difficulty or egg drop continues beyond a few days.
prevention: Maintain consistent, adequate ventilation year-round.
Avoid sudden temperature changes and overcrowding.
Practice all-in/all-out flock management where possible.
Keep housing and equipment clean and disinfected regularly.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Seek veterinary assessment if respiratory signs worsen, spread through the flock, or egg production does not recover within one to two weeks.

diseases.name: Newcastle Disease (ND)
recommendedActions: Isolate affected birds immediately and limit movement in and out of the coop.
Avoid bringing in new birds until the flock's health status is confirmed.
Contact your local Department of Agriculture / Bureau of Animal Industry office promptly.
Disinfect equipment, footwear, and housing to limit spread.
prevention: Follow a Newcastle Disease vaccination schedule appropriate for your flock.
Practice strict biosecurity — limit visitors and disinfect before entering the coop.
Quarantine new or returning birds before introducing them to the flock.
Monitor the flock daily for early respiratory or nervous signs.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Newcastle Disease is a notifiable disease in the Philippines. Contact your local DA/BAI veterinary office promptly — do not rely on home management alone.

diseases.name: Infectious Coryza
recommendedActions: Isolate affected birds to reduce spread within the flock.
Gently clean facial discharge before any veterinarian-guided treatment.
Improve coop ventilation and reduce overcrowding.
Consult a veterinarian for appropriate treatment and flock management.
prevention: Avoid mixing birds of different ages or unknown health status.
Maintain good ventilation and reduce dust and ammonia buildup.
Practice regular coop sanitation and equipment disinfection.
Isolate and observe new birds before adding them to the flock.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Consult a veterinarian if facial swelling worsens, spreads to more birds, or appetite does not improve.

diseases.name: Fowl Cholera (Pasteurellosis)
recommendedActions: Isolate affected birds — fowl cholera can spread and progress quickly.
Disinfect housing, feeders, and waterers thoroughly.
Monitor the rest of the flock closely for similar signs.
Seek prompt veterinary evaluation and guidance.
prevention: Control rodents and wild bird contact, common sources of spread.
Avoid overcrowding and maintain good sanitation.
Remove and properly dispose of any deceased birds promptly.
Discuss vaccination options with a veterinarian if cholera is recurring in your area.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Seek veterinary attention promptly — fowl cholera can progress rapidly and cause sudden losses if untreated.

diseases.name: Coccidiosis
recommendedActions: Keep litter and bedding dry — coccidia spread readily in wet, dirty conditions.
Isolate visibly unwell birds and monitor droppings closely.
Ensure consistent access to clean water and feed.
Consult a veterinarian or feed supplier about appropriate anticoccidial support.
prevention: Keep litter dry and replace wet or soiled bedding promptly.
Avoid overcrowding, which increases contamination risk.
Clean and disinfect feeders and waterers regularly.
Consider coccidiosis-resistant feed programs for young birds.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Consult a veterinarian if bloody or persistent diarrhea, or noticeable weight loss, is observed.

diseases.name: Fowl Pox
recommendedActions: Isolate affected birds to limit spread through direct contact or mosquitoes.
Keep lesions clean and dry; avoid picking at scabs.
Control mosquito populations around the coop.
Consult a veterinarian if lesions spread to the mouth or affect breathing.
prevention: Reduce standing water and mosquito breeding sites near the coop.
Disinfect housing and equipment regularly.
Isolate new birds before introducing them to the flock.
Discuss fowl pox vaccination with a veterinarian if recurring in your area.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Most cases are mild and self-resolving, but seek veterinary advice if lesions spread to the mouth/throat or breathing becomes difficult.

diseases.name: Chronic Respiratory Disease (CRD)
recommendedActions: Reduce stress factors such as overcrowding and poor ventilation.
Isolate affected birds to reduce spread.
Maintain clean, dust-reduced housing conditions.
Consult a veterinarian, especially if signs recur frequently.
prevention: Minimize overcrowding and maintain good airflow.
Reduce dust and ammonia buildup through regular cleaning.
Avoid mixing birds from different sources.
Address stress factors like sudden temperature or feed changes.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: CRD tends to recur under stress. Consult a veterinarian if symptoms are frequent or persistent despite management changes.

diseases.name: Fowl Typhoid (Salmonella Gallinarum)
recommendedActions: Isolate affected birds and disinfect housing and equipment.
Monitor the rest of the flock closely for similar signs.
Maintain clean feed and water sources to limit spread.
Seek prompt veterinary evaluation.
prevention: Source birds and hatching eggs from reputable, disease-free suppliers.
Practice strict sanitation for feeders, waterers, and housing.
Control rodents, which can carry and spread Salmonella.
Quarantine new birds before adding them to the flock.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Seek veterinary attention promptly, as fowl typhoid can cause rising mortality once birds become symptomatic.

diseases.name: Infectious Synovitis (Mycoplasma synoviae)
recommendedActions: Isolate affected birds to reduce joint strain and spread.
Provide soft, clean bedding to ease movement and reduce injury.
Ensure feed and water are easily reachable for less mobile birds.
Consult a veterinarian for evaluation of joint swelling and lameness.
prevention: Source birds from flocks with known clean health status.
Practice good sanitation to reduce secondary infection risk.
Avoid overcrowding, which increases contact-based spread.
Monitor young birds closely, as they are commonly affected.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Consult a veterinarian if lameness worsens, affects multiple birds, or is accompanied by visible joint swelling.

diseases.name: External Parasite Infestation (Mites / Lice)
recommendedActions: Inspect birds closely, especially around the vent and under wings, for parasites.
Clean and disinfect housing, perches, and nesting areas thoroughly.
Provide a dust-bathing area, which helps birds naturally manage parasites.
Consult a veterinarian or poultry supplier for appropriate parasite control options.
prevention: Clean and disinfect coops and equipment on a regular schedule.
Provide accessible dust-bathing areas for the flock.
Inspect new birds before introducing them to the flock.
Control wild bird access, which can introduce parasites.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Consult a veterinarian or agricultural extension office if infestation is severe or feather loss is extensive.

diseases.name: Avian Influenza (HPAI)
recommendedActions: Stop handling birds beyond what is necessary and avoid moving them off the property.
Isolate the affected area and limit access to the coop.
Contact your local Department of Agriculture / Bureau of Animal Industry office immediately.
Avoid contact between the affected flock and other poultry or wild birds.
prevention: Practice strict biosecurity, including limiting visitor and vehicle access.
Prevent contact between backyard flocks and wild birds or waterfowl.
Report unusual illness or sudden deaths to DA/BAI promptly.
Avoid bringing in birds from markets or sources of unknown health status.
diseases.veterinaryGuidance: Avian Influenza is a notifiable, reportable disease in the Philippines. Report immediately to your local DA/BAI veterinary office — do not attempt home management.
